entities.name: Siddhartha Gautama (Buddha)
entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Siddhartha Gautama (c. 563–483 BCE), known as the Buddha (‘the Awakened One’), was a Shakya prince born in Lumbini (modern Nepal) whose renunciation of royal privilege and subsequent spiritual awakening launched Buddhism — today the world’s fourth-largest religion with over 500 million adherents. Raised in luxury by King Suddhodana, the young prince was shielded from suffering until four encounters (an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and an ascetic) shattered his illusions at age 29, prompting the Great Renunciation. After six years of extreme asceticism, near-starvation, and study under leading teachers, he rejected both indulgence and self-mortification in favor of the Middle Way. At age 35, meditating beneath the Bodhi Tree in Bodh Gaya, he attained supreme enlightenment (sambodhi), perceiving the Four Noble Truths: suffering (dukkha) exists, it arises from craving (tanha), it can cease (nirodha), and the path to cessation is the Noble Eightfold Path. His first sermon at the Deer Park in Sarnath (‘Setting the Wheel of Dharma in Motion’) established the Sangha (monastic community), and for 45 years he traversed the Gangetic plain teaching kings, merchants, outcasts, and women alike — extraordinary for his era’s rigid caste system. The Buddha’s teachings were preserved orally and later compiled into the Tripitaka (Pali Canon), the oldest complete Buddhist scripture. Emperor Ashoka’s conversion (c. 260 BCE) transformed Buddhism from a regional Indian movement into a pan-Asian civilization force, spreading to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China, Korea, Japan, and Southeast Asia. The Buddha’s insights on impermanence (anicca), non-self (anatta), and dependent origination (pratityasamutpada) anticipated modern psychology, cognitive science, and mindfulness-based therapeutic approaches by 2,500 years.
